title: Chapter 6: Enums, Records, and Sealed Types
description: Represent closed choices and transparent values with Java 21 language features. The learner builds behavior-bearing enums, validates and defensively copies record components, constrains extension with sealed hierarchies, writes exhaustive pattern switches, and defends when an ordinary class is a more honest model.

lessons.title: Sealed classes and controlled extension
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Sealed classes and controlled extension

## A controlled family of alternatives
A sealed hierarchy says which direct subtypes are allowed.
```java
sealed interface Result permits Success, Failure {}
record Success(String value) implements Result {}
record Failure(String reason) implements Result {}
```
Records are implicitly final, satisfying the requirement that a permitted subtype decide whether extension stops or continues. An ordinary permitted subtype must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. In a named module permitted types belong to that module; in an unnamed module they belong to the same package.

## Model alternatives with their own data
A Result has either a successful value or a failure reason. A class containing successFlag, value, and error allows contradictory combinations; separate variants make those combinations harder to construct. Sealing supports exhaustive decisions, while an open interface supports implementations you do not know about.

## Practice
Model a payment result as Accepted(receiptId), Declined(reason), and Pending(reference). State validation rules for each component. Decide whether plugins should be able to add variants; if so, sealing may be the wrong extension contract. Add a fourth variant and observe which exhaustive consumers require updates.

exercises.title: Sealed classes and controlled extension: concept check
hints: Recall that a sealed type's permits clause enumerates its allowed direct subtypes; it says nothing about caller access or how many instances exist.

exercises.instructionMarkdown: Does an exhaustive subtype switch automatically accept null?
choices: Yes; null means the default subtype
No; null needs its own policy
Yes; null matches the first subtype
hints: Recall that instanceof and pattern switch treat null as its own case; matching every listed subtype does not implicitly cover a null selector.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 assessment and deliberate practice
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Chapter 6 assessment

Draw on this chapter's coverage of enums, records, sealed hierarchies, and pattern switches to work through the decision scenario and repair **Defensive record components**, a lab where a record's canonical constructor must guard against a caller-supplied mutable list. Write a prediction before running the debugger and preserve the intended snapshot behavior when fixing it.

The function exercise is a bounded practice task, not proof of every chapter competency. Complete the implementation and external practice described in the five lessons as well. Review the changed source for its contract, then explain the relevant tradeoff without consulting the answer.

choices: Whether and how to copy and protect its contents
Whether the record keyword is capitalized

exercises.title: Chapter 6 implementation lab: status
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `status`. Map NEW to queued and DONE to completed; return unknown for every other case. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Only NEW and DONE have mappings in this exercise; all other text, including ACTIVE, returns unknown.
hints: Map exactly the two named inputs, NEW and DONE, to their outputs; every other text, including a valid-looking state like ACTIVE, falls through to unknown.
Trace both public-style examples plus a case-sensitivity boundary such as "done" and the empty string before submitting.

exercises.title: Defensive record components
exercises.instructionMarkdown: The `Team` record stores the caller's mutable list reference directly instead of snapshotting it, so clearing the input list after construction empties the record's view too and the program no longer writes `1`. Repair the constructor so it defensively copies the list, keeping the demonstrated construction call, and explain why copying restores the expected size; do not replace it with a hard-coded print. Output tests verify the result; preserving the intended operation requires source review.
hints: The record must snapshot its mutable input.
